difficultyRationale: Requires reasoning about worst-case tree shape rather than reciting the average-case search behavior, which is the interview-level depth this distinguishes.
prompt: A backend service stores millions of sorted keys in a binary search tree (BST) to support range queries. If keys are inserted in strictly increasing order with no rebalancing, what happens to the worst-case lookup time, and why does this matter for reasoning about self-balancing trees (such as red-black or AVL trees)?
explanation: Inserting keys in strictly increasing order into a plain BST with no rebalancing produces a tree that is effectively a chain, equivalent in shape to a linked list, so lookup degrades to O(n) in the worst case. Self-balancing trees matter precisely because they maintain a height bound of O(log n) regardless of insertion order, guaranteeing worst-case lookup rather than depending on favorable input.

options.text: The tree always stays O(log n) because a BST is defined by its sorted (in-order) property, not by its shape.
options.explanation: The sorted in-order traversal property is maintained regardless of shape, but lookup time depends on the tree's height, which is a function of shape; a skewed shape can have height n even though the in-order property still holds.

options.text: The tree degenerates into a chain equivalent to a linked list, making lookup O(n) in the worst case; self-balancing trees guarantee O(log n) height regardless of insertion order.
options.explanation: Correct: with no rebalancing, each new larger key becomes the right child of the previous maximum, producing a single chain of height n, so lookup is O(n); self-balancing trees restructure on insertion specifically to avoid this.

options.text: Self-balancing trees improve average-case insertion to O(1) by caching the most recently inserted node for faster future access.
options.explanation: This describes no real mechanism used by self-balancing trees. Their insertion cost is O(log n), not O(1), and they don't cache a 'most recent' node for shortcutting future operations.

options.text: The worst case for a strictly-increasing-order BST is still O(log n), because each key comparison halves the remaining search space just like binary search on a sorted array, where comparing against the middle element always discards half of the remaining candidates regardless of how the array was originally populated.
options.explanation: This is the exact misconception the scenario is testing: halving the search space only happens when the tree is reasonably balanced. A degenerate chain-shaped tree does not halve anything per comparison, since every node has only one child.
